toc.title: An experiment you can do yourself
RSA is not essential to the theory
Who the paper is really written for

blocks.p: Despite what you may have heard recently, no, the Polyvagal Theory is not dead.

I'm a member of the Polyvagal Institute's editorial board. That means I'm one of a handful of people who review other people's work for Polyvagal Theory accuracy, and the theory has been a huge part of this podcast for years now.

Am I biased? Yeah, I am. You can probably hear it in my voice. I'm a little annoyed by this stuff. But I am much more interested in what's true. So yes, I'm biased, but I want truth, or at least as close to the truth as we can get. Things need to make sense to me. Hear out my arguments and decide for yourself.

The writer of the article is Paul Grossman, and the article is called "Why the Polyvagal Theory is Untenable." Grossman has been a Polyvagal Theory critic for a very, very long time. Stephen Porges, the creator of the Polyvagal Theory, has replied to these criticisms numerous times over many, many years. Porges has even chatted with me on my podcast about these criticisms.

Dr. Porges said: "I don't mind criticizing people's science, but I don't like to go on an offense where saying people are blatantly wrong. But it's really quite remarkable: for over about a 20-year period, a couple of people were repeatedly misrepresenting the theory and publishing statements that were creating what is classically called a strawman argument."
He's not shying away from them.

I'm a therapist, and even though my knowledge on the topic is deep, I'm going to stay in my lane. I won't address which of these two I think is right. But I will use critical thinking and simply check their work, and that's going to tell us a lot.

You and I don't need to be experts in the Polyvagal Theory, actually. All we need to do is look at the new paper's claims about the Polyvagal Theory and check whether Grossman accurately understands the theory. If he does not accurately understand the theory, then his counterarguments are kind of moot, right? At that point, he's arguing against his own interpretation, not the theory itself. This is extremely important.

Dr. Porges said: "So they make the false statement, they say, this isn't true. Well, the theory never said that, and I would agree with them that that's not true either. But then they would go on and on with these things."

So let's start from the very beginning of the polyvagal of it all: the vagal paradox. This question is what drove the creation of the Polyvagal Theory, so understanding it is obviously very important.

Grossman says, and this is a quote, that the vagal paradox, "often mentioned by Porges to indicate that RSA," which is respiratory sinus arrhythmia, "sometimes correlates with changes in cardiac vagal tone and other times fails to, is not paradoxical at all when RSA is no longer equated with cardiac vagal tone, but when RSA is realistically considered as a vulnerable and approximate index of cardiac vagal tone, constrained in its accuracy by many factors."

That sounds good, right? It's kind of intimidating, lots of fancy words. The only problem is that's not what the vagal paradox is. I'm not going to speak for Porges, of course. I'm simply going to quote him from his paper called "The Vagal Paradox." He says: "How could the vagus be both protective when it was expressed as RSA and life-threatening when it was expressed as bradycardia and apnea?"

So what's the problem here? Grossman is fundamentally misidentifying what the vagal paradox actually is. He reframes it as a measurement problem. He is essentially arguing that it's just a methodological limitation of RSA as an index of cardiac vagal tone. In his framing, there's no real paradox, just an imprecise measuring tool. RSA is a measuring tool. But that's not the paradox that Porges identified.

The actual vagal paradox, as Porges articulated it, is a question about neurobiology: how the same nerve, the vagus, can be both life sustaining when expressed as RSA, which indicates healthy vagal tone and resilience, and life threatening when it's expressed as bradycardia and apnea, which can kill a preterm infant.

These are two completely different questions. Let me reword it one more time. Grossman's version is: is RSA a good enough ruler for measuring vagal tone? Porges' actual version is: why does the same nerve produce opposite survival outcomes?

The vagal paradox drove Porges to investigate the brainstem, and ultimately to discover that there are two anatomically distinct vagal pathways, originating from different brainstem nuclei, with fundamentally different functions, both of which use the vagus nerve.

A personal thought: I find it very, very odd that Grossman did not include a direct quote from Porges about the vagal paradox in this critique paper. It took me 30 seconds. It's really not hard. Porges has a paper called "The Vagal Paradox." I imagine if Grossman had reread that paper, he would have realized that he misunderstood. I would hope.

I also find it odd that Grossman dismisses the bradycardia piece of Porges' question. The Polyvagal Theory hypothesizes that the vagus nerve serves as the highway for two heart rate influences, ventral and dorsal. That's the theory derived from the vagal paradox. Why does Grossman ignore bradycardia in his definition of the vagal paradox? He didn't mention it at all. Either he doesn't get it or he's ignoring it.

Remember, Grossman is responding to Porges' vagal paradox question. Grossman does not have his own vagal paradox, as best I can tell. So to respond to Porges' question, Grossman needs to accurately understand it, right? So why doesn't he accurately express Porges' vagal paradox to set up his rebuttal? And another reminder: Porges has responded to this guy numerous times. There is no excuse for this misunderstanding.

blocks.h: An experiment you can do yourself

blocks.p: I knew this already because I'm familiar with both of them, but I took it a step further and did a really easy experiment that you can do yourself. Download Grossman's paper, then download Porges' paper. Upload them to a non-biased AI. I used Google NotebookLM, which is amazing at using sources and has a huge context for exactly this purpose. Then ask it to give you the definitions from Grossman and Porges.
And guess what? The AI defines Porges' definition as protection versus threat, and Grossman's definition as a measurement misunderstanding.

You could do this little experiment yourself with any questions you have about their work: how it's misaligned, who misunderstands what, or just to understand it better. Don't taint the AI. Just ask it objective questions, and ask it to give you the answer at like a fifth-grade reading level.

blocks.h: RSA is not essential to the theory

blocks.p: Grossman spends a lot of time on RSA in this paper. He treats RSA as a foundational construct of the Polyvagal Theory. Basically, if he can break down the RSA argument, then the theory crumbles. I think that's what he's getting at.

However, Porges said in his 2023 paper, quote, "RSA is a portal to the function of the ventral vagus enabling the testing of polyvagal-informed hypotheses, but is not a foundational construct of the theory." Porges uses RSA as a potential measurement of something very specific. Very specific. If that measurement doesn't work out, it doesn't mean the entire theory is untenable.

Think of it this way. Let's say you hypothesized that the temperature of someone's forehead correlates with how sick they are. You use a thermometer as your measurement tool. Now somebody comes along and says that thermometer is not perfectly accurate. It gives inconsistent readings depending on ambient temperature and sweat and skin tone. Therefore, the concept of illness is untenable.

That sounds absurd, right? The thermometer is just one potential portal into detecting something real. Attacking the instrument doesn't dissolve the underlying phenomenon. That's exactly what Grossman is doing with RSA. RSA is Porges' thermometer, a portal, to use his own word, into detecting ventral vagal activity. It's a useful, testable, measurable, repeatable window into something the theory proposes is real. But the Polyvagal Theory does not stand or fall on whether RSA is a perfect index of cardiac vagal tone.

The theory's foundational constructs are neuroanatomical and evolutionary: the existence of two distinct vagal pathways, the evolutionary hierarchy of the autonomic nervous system, and the adaptive functions of each circuit. Those claims live in the brainstem, not in a heart rate variability graph.

So when Grossman dedicates really substantial effort to dismantling RSA as a reliable measure, he's essentially arguing that the thermometer is flawed and concluding that fever does not exist. Again, I don't understand why Grossman would go to such effort to dismantle RSA when Porges has said that it's not central to his theory.

The third issue I'll tackle is freeze and shutdown. Listeners of this podcast will know the difference between freeze and shutdown very well, but for anyone new: freeze and shutdown are not the same thing.

They both involve immobility, yes, and they're both autonomically driven. But shutdown is a limp collapse, and freeze is a tense paralysis. Shutdown would be like playing dead and falling to the floor. Freeze is like a panic attack. It's tense.

In the Polyvagal Theory, shutdown is a dorsal vagal response. Freeze is a dorsal vagal response plus sympathetic flight or fight. Grossman confuses the two, and I don't even entirely blame him for this, because Porges' language on the subject was very confusing in his primary writings. I asked him about this way back in episode 15, during my first interview with him, and he did clarify the distinction.

Dr. Porges said: "So there's this whole ambiguity because people use the word freeze when they really mean shutting down. Okay? So the mouse in the jaws of a cat is not frozen, it's just limp. And that is clearly the limp loss of muscle tone, is a dorsal vagal response. The rigidity is much more, let's say, okay, mixed or complex."

Porges says that bradycardia reflects dorsal vagal influence, as a measurement. Bradycardia is a significantly slower heartbeat, which is potentially fatal. In shutdown, a dorsal vagal response, we would expect to see bradycardia. We would expect to see a massive drop in heart rate, just like Porges saw in the neonatal unit with the preterm infants that prompted the vagal paradox.

But what about freeze? Would we expect to see a massive drop in heart rate during freeze? Again, freeze is the combination of immobility and mobility: shutdown plus flight or fight, dorsal plus sympathetic. Both pathways are active at the same time.

Freeze can look like a panic attack, or scared stiff, or tonic immobility. So outwardly it's immobile, but internally there's a high level of activation, including a higher heart rate. So no, I don't think we would expect to see bradycardia in freeze. Grossman does not understand this, and argues that there is no bradycardia in freeze.
I assume Porges' response would be, "Yeah. No kidding."

Next topic: non-mammals and myelinated nerves that affect heart rate. Grossman points to extensive research showing that non-mammalian species, such as sharks and fish and reptiles, also possess fast-acting myelinated nerves and can use them to instantly change their heart rate in response to their environment.

From Grossman's perspective, because this hardware exists throughout the vertebrate family tree, it cannot be a special mammalian innovation for social engagement, as Porges suggests. But this is not a Polyvagal Theory proposition. Porges has already clarified that the Polyvagal Theory does not rely on mammals being the only ones with fast-acting nerves that slow down heart rate. It doesn't matter if non-mammals can slow their heart with fast-acting myelinated nerves. It doesn't matter.

Instead, the Polyvagal Theory focuses on the brainstem regions where those nerves originate. Porges argues that in mammals, these nerves underwent an evolutionary ventral migration to the front of the brainstem, moving from the dorsal motor nucleus to the nucleus ambiguus. This shift is critical, because it places the heart's braking system right next to the nerves that control the face, voice, and listening.

That brings us to the next issue, which is Grossman's misunderstanding about social behavior. He points out that modern reptiles are far from asocial creatures. They exhibit complex behaviors such as long-term pair bonding, communal parenting, and social learning. That was actually really interesting. I wasn't aware of these things.

But in response, Porges says that's cool about the reptiles, but it's also entirely irrelevant to the Polyvagal Theory, which he describes as mammal-centric. He clarifies that the Polyvagal Theory is interested in the specific evolutionary transition from ancient, extinct common ancestors to mammals, not the separate path that modern reptiles took. The sociality of modern reptiles is irrelevant.

Mammals have a unique social engagement system, according to the Polyvagal Theory. This system integrates heart regulation with facial expressions and voice, giving mammals the ability to use social cues, like a warm voice, gentle eye contact, eye crinkles, or smiling, to help calm each other and to indicate safety. This is called co-regulation.

Porges' social engagement system, co-regulation, is not the same, I don't think, as Grossman's social behaviors in reptiles. Just think about it for a second. When was the last time you saw iguanas smiling at each other, or heard a snake singing to its young to calm them? How about two frogs embracing closely in the moonlight?
Grossman does not accurately reflect Porges' social engagement system. The sociality he's discussing is obviously different. These are not the same thing.

blocks.h: Who the paper is really written for

blocks.p: Grossman and friends have more to say. I assume Porges is going to respond yet again, but honestly, if he doesn't, I don't blame him. And since recording this, I found that Porges has already released a rebuttal. I wasn't even aware of it. So there may be even better arguments in it than the ones I've covered here.

Grossman is recycling the same talking points he has harped on for years on ResearchGate, taking them to the general public, begging for others to interact with him, to respond to him, to debate him. No, I'm not exaggerating. Read it for yourself.

Did Grossman collect a few dozen others to edit and sign this paper? Yeah. And that's something. But the paper largely doesn't address what the Polyvagal Theory actually says. So I don't know what that's worth.

Scientists get things wrong. It has happened throughout history, especially when new ideas surface that contradict traditional understandings and the status quo. And scientific debate is totally fine.

But one thing really sticks out to me about this specific paper from Grossman and friends. It seems to be written with a psychological bent. It doesn't seem to be written for the science crowd, exactly. I mean, it kind of is, because it uses all the science terminology. But it also singles out people like me, who use the theory to better understand and help our clients. The paper addresses people like me in the abstract and in the introduction as well.

It seems pretty clear to me that this is who it's written for. It doesn't seem to be written for Dr. Porges. There are no new arguments in it for him to rebut. It's the same stuff over and over again. It's written for mental health service providers, which I find really interesting.

The last three of its 12 conclusions are about psychology and treatment, and they encourage people like me to look elsewhere, to disregard the Polyvagal Theory. What's sad is that it seems to have worked. Therapists and psychologists and the like seem to be responding by abandoning the theory, except for the stuff they like, such as the states and co-regulation, because Grossman's paper seems scary. It seems like he gets the theory, has counterarguments, and has a few dozen people who agree. Therapists, even popular YouTube therapists and Instagram therapy influencers, are not spending the time to examine it.

And mostly I don't blame them. It's really difficult. It's very dense. Reading people who disagree is not easy. But a lot of what I pointed out here just requires a smidge of research and critical thinking. It's really not that hard. You don't have to be an expert in neuroanatomy to say, this dude does not understand what this other dude is saying. And you really don't need to be an expert, in 2026, to upload two scientific papers into an unbiased AI and ask your own questions. I think it's actually a really good idea.

Does any of this mean I know for certain that what Dr. Porges says is true? No. No, it doesn't. I'm a layperson. But what he writes about makes sense to me, and honestly, it has made more sense in the psychology realm than anything else I've learned about. And it's not a modality. It's the science that contributes to the way we think about things.

The serious criticisms of the Polyvagal Theory, which really all come from Grossman, who cites someone named Taylor all the time, really don't measure up. I hope you can see that from just this one piece. I don't think I'll continue commenting on this. I don't really have much more to say about it. If you have follow-up questions, I'd recommend reading Dr. Porges' direct responses to Grossman. That would be the best place to go.
I think the Polyvagal Theory bandwagon is disappearing, and I love it.
